item.title: Hala Mobility combines EV rentals, delivery jobs, and financial services for gig workers
item.description: Hala Mobility gives delivery riders EV rentals, delivery jobs, early-salary financing and accident insurance, says founder Srikanth Reddy Kalakonda.
item.content:encoded:
Delivery riders can cover 100 to 120 km a day, often on petrol vehicles that aren’t designed for such intensive use. Rising fuel prices add to their operating costs.

Electric vehicles (EVs) can reduce these expenses, and delivery companies are encouraging riders to make the switch. However, riders who cannot afford or access an EV have little choice but to continue using petrol vehicles.

Access to a vehicle is only part of the problem. Riders also need to know how far it can travel on a charge, where to charge it, and where to get it serviced. For companies managing large EV fleets, the challenges extend to monitoring battery health, battery swaps, energy consumption, and maintenance schedules.

Hyderabad-based Hala Mobility aims to address these gaps through an EV fleet-as-a-service and multi-modal shared mobility platform that allows riders and delivery companies to use EVs without purchasing them.

Through the Hala app, riders can rent, lease or finance vehicles. Hala was founded in 2019 by Srikanth Reddy Kalakonda, Founder and CEO, and Co-founder Snehith Reddy Meda.

Kalakonda studied computer science at Jawaharlal Nehru Technological University and completed master's degrees at the University of Padua and the Polytechnic University of Madrid. He later pursued a PhD, during which he developed Chippy, a mobility aggregator app.

Meda studied electronics and communication engineering at Manipal Institute of Technology and founded the agritech company OneBasket.

Vehicles, jobs, and financial support

Hala works with riders through two models.

For delivery companies such as Zomato, Swiggy and Zepto, it provides both riders and electric vehicles and manages operations. Delivery companies pay Hala for each order completed. Hala deducts vehicle rental and related costs and passes the remaining amount, including incentives, to the rider.

“Everything is passed on. There is no commission,” Kalakonda says.

Riders who already have delivery jobs can subscribe to a vehicle for a week, 15 days or a month. Hala’s website lists rentals starting at Rs 189 a day and three-month leases from Rs 13,999.

Kalakonda describes the business as a combination of vehicle rentals, logistics, and platform services, designed to keep vehicles in use.

Hala also allows riders to work with at least three delivery companies, enabling them to switch between platforms depending on order availability. According to Kalakonda, the average rider on its platform earns close to Rs 32,000 a month.

The startup uses data such as timely rental payments, order volumes, and customer ratings to score riders. These scores help connect them with financiers offering early-salary advances.

Kalakonda says every rider also receives accident insurance, underwritten using the same data, with Rs 5 lakh in coverage in the event of death.

About 90% of Hala's customers are gig workers who have migrated from other parts of the country and lack stable housing, which Kalakonda says affects their health.

To address this, Hala is developing Blue Base, a community hub offering charging, parking, vehicle servicing, and housing for riders.

Blue Base also plans to operate vehicles in shifts of eight to nine hours, allowing another rider to use a vehicle while the first rider rests.

Managing the fleet with data

Hala uses an internal software platform called Circle OS to track vehicles throughout their lifecycle, from deployment and servicing to refurbishment or scrapping.

Kalakonda says the system uses AI to analyse nine to 10 inputs, including data related to drivers, vehicles, charging stations, service centres, inventory, and order patterns.

The software helps Hala predict and extend vehicle life, determine when a vehicle can be refurbished instead of scrapped, and compare operating costs with rental income.

Each vehicle is fitted with an Internet of Things (IoT) telematics device that transmits data every five seconds.

Riders use this information to check a vehicle’s remaining range, identify faults, and locate the nearest service station. When a battery runs low, the app directs them to a nearby charging station and shows how many drivers are waiting.

“Every data point has to be tracked, traced, monitored, and controlled,” Kalakonda says.

He puts fleet utilisation at nearly 88% and uptime at 94%.

What growth looks like

Hala's business clients include Zomato, Swiggy, Zepto, Blinkit, BigBasket, Amazon, Flipkart, and Porter. Individual riders account for the rest of its customers.

Its fleet grew from 2,484 vehicles in March 2025 to more than 8,100 in March 2026. The company now operates nearly 18,000 vehicles across nine cities.

Kalakonda says Hala has been EBITDA-positive since its inception and profit-after-tax positive for the past two financial years. The startup reported revenue of Rs 96 crore in the last financial year and is targeting Rs 262 crore to Rs 270 crore this year.

It has raised approximately Rs 21 crore in equity and Rs 70 crore in debt. Hala is also part of the 2025 cohort of the ClimaFii Alliance, a programme run in India by Upaya Social Ventures. The startup is currently raising a Rs 135-crore Series A round to fund its financing, insurance and housing initiatives.

Kalakonda expects Hala to have around 50,000 vehicles on the road within a year and aims to build a profitable listed company by 2030 or 2031.

Beyond rentals, leasing, and delivery services, he wants Hala to become a broader support system for gig workers. “This is my safety net, and this is where I belong,” Kalakonda says, describing how he wants riders to feel about the platform.

item.title: From local roots to national reach: How three Rajasthan startups are scaling beyond the state
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, founders of ChurningMind, SafeSpace Personal Wellness, and HNNOIX shared how they are taking solutions built for farmers, students, and telecom networks from Rajasthan to national and global markets.
item.content:encoded:
Ask three Rajasthan founders what got them started, and you hear about three very different problems. Many farmers in the state still pay to get their produce graded before they can sell it. In Kota, India’s coaching capital, student mental health has drawn scrutiny all the way up to the Supreme Court. And most of the technology behind the 5G icon on an Indian phone screen comes from abroad.

For the founders on stage at TechSparks 2026, each of these became the starting point of a startup that began in Rajasthan and is now reaching well beyond it.

In a panel titled ‘From local roots to national reach: Scaling startups from Rajasthan’, Nishant Gupta, Co-founder of ChurningMind; Siddharth Pathak, Founder of SafeSpace Personal Wellness; and Hargovind Bansal, Founder and CEO of HNNOIX, spoke with Dhawal Singhal, Program Manager at iStart Rajasthan, about building for hard-to-reach users and scaling from a Tier II base.

iStart is the Rajasthan government’s startup program, run by the Department of IT & Communication. Singhal said it now has more than 9,400 registered startups and offers incubation, grants of up to Rs 60 lakh, and a Rs 100 crore fund of funds. It also lets government departments give startups work orders directly instead of through standard tenders.

Building AI for the farmer, not the demo

ChurningMind is building AI for people in rural India across agriculture, health, labour, education, and geospatial intelligence. Gupta said the goal is to bring them under one umbrella so that no one feels left out, from farmers to migrant workers moving between states and rural women who struggle to access healthcare or government schemes.

Asked what it takes to move from a demo to a product people can depend on, Gupta pointed to language. Rural users speak regional languages, so ChurningMind is working on real-time voice-to-voice translation. The aim is for a farmer in a remote part of Rajasthan to talk directly to a farmer in Odisha, each in their own language, without needing English or Hindi.

Its flagship agriculture platform tackles a more basic problem. Farmers often have to pay to get their produce graded before they can approach traders. Gupta said younger farmers now use 4G and 5G phones, and ChurningMind uses that access to offer real-time crop scanning, market prices, and trader connections across India, not just in their own district. The platform links farmers, farmer producer organizations (FPOs), mandis, exporters, traders, and government agencies.

ChurningMind is also working with the Rajasthan government on e-governance, Gupta said, aimed at setting a benchmark that can be adopted nationally.

“You have to keep churning about how you can serve better,” he said, explaining the company’s name.

Mental health support that knows when to step back

Pathak’s path to founding SafeSpace began with his own setback. He spent five years preparing for the civil services exam but did not clear it, and said it left him with low self-esteem until a friend studying psychology helped him through it. He later joined a certification program in agentic AI and built a prototype in three months.

SafeSpace is a proactive, AI-powered mental health platform for students. Users log their mood daily, and AI tracks patterns over time. Real psychologists stay in the loop: if the AI detects a crisis, the user is connected to a professional, and if a student’s weekly trend dips, a psychologist reaches out.

Rajasthan, home to the coaching hub of Kota, has faced intense scrutiny over student mental health. In September 2025, the state passed the Rajasthan Coaching Centres (Control and Regulation) Bill, which provides for a state-level portal and a 24x7 counselling helpline for students.

Pathak said he is working closely with the state’s higher education department, which is building a portal for coaching institutions.

Research with SafeSpace’s clinical psychologists surprised him. Relationship issues, not studies, were students’ top mental health concern; studies ranked fifth. Parents, he said, were among the strongest supporters. “Our children don’t talk to us,” he recalled parents telling him. Many wanted their children to have a professional to talk to, even if it was not them.

SafeSpace started as a direct-to-consumer app but shifted to selling to institutions. The Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) now requires affiliated schools to appoint one counselling and wellness teacher for every 500 students, under a circular issued in January 2026 following a public interest litigation in the Rajasthan High Court.

Pathak said many school counsellors are underused, so SafeSpace offers schools a dashboard with anonymous, class-level data to help them reach students who need support.

Talking about how SafeSpace prevents students from becoming emotionally dependent on an AI chatbot, Pathak said the platform caps daily conversations at 30. Students with serious concerns are directed to a psychologist or to Tele MANAS, the government’s 24-hour mental health helpline, which SafeSpace has integrated. Tele MANAS has received more than 47 lakh calls since it launched in October 2022.

“I want to normalize mental health, not as a rich people thing,” he said, adding that he wants government schools and colleges to have the same access as private ones.

Putting India at the 6G standards table

Bansal, who grew up in a small town in Rajasthan, spent 17 years in the US innovation ecosystem working on 4G, 5G, location, and healthcare technologies. He said that work led to more than 350 patents filed and granted in over 15 countries.

He returned to build HNNOIX, a deeptech company developing AI-native 6G technology. His motivation was: the phones in people’s pockets and the 4G and 5G networks they run on are largely built on foreign technology, and India pays high royalties as a result.

Bansal explained standardization with a school uniform analogy. Just as students follow a set uniform, technologies such as 4G, 5G or satellite communications must follow global standards so devices from different makers work together. Companies present their technology to global bodies such as 3GPP and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), and accepted technologies become standards, which adds value to the country behind them.

India’s participation in 3GPP has grown quickly. The number of Indian participants rose from 717 in 2020 to 1,787 in 2025, while technical contributions increased from 196 to 2,943 over the same period. Under the Bharat 6G Vision, India aims to contribute at least 10% of global 6G standards and patents. HNNOIX holds 3GPP membership with support from the Department of Telecommunications and represents India as part of government delegations at the ITU, Bansal said.

Asked what pays the bills when 6G is years away, Bansal said building a generation of telecom technology takes seven to eight years. Work on 5G, he noted, began around 2012, well before South Korea launched the first commercial networks in 2019. India adopted 4G and 5G after other countries had already built them. With 6G expected to be deployed globally around 2030, India is choosing to participate from the start.

HNNOIX is also driving a mission to develop one lakh technology inventors by 2030, which Bansal said was presented to the prime minister last year. The company has reached more than 50,000 learners across every state and union territory and filed more than 200 patents in India, the US and Europe, he said. No single company can build that capability alone, he added, which is why HNNOIX works with institutions to develop inventors.

Starting a company with global customers such as Apple and Samsung from Rajasthan was tough, he admitted. With no similar startup in India, people struggled to understand the idea. Bansal saw that as both a challenge and an opportunity, since it also meant there were no competitors. Over time, he said, iStart helped with mentorship, connections to institutions, and introductions to the central government, including nominations for international delegations.

Lessons for founders from smaller cities

Each founder closed with one takeaway for founders building outside metros.

Gupta, a data scientist with a master’s degree from the US and 15 years of work experience, said his journey from the US to learning from farmers in rural Rajasthan has shaped his goal: helping farmers become agripreneurs known across India and globally.

Bansal urged founders not to let challenges stop them before they start. “Dream big. Do not see the challenges when you start something,” he said. “You motivate yourself by looking at the success stories, not the failure stories.”

Pathak returned to access, saying mental health support should reach every student, regardless of the school they attend.

Together, their stories made a case that a Rajasthan address is no barrier to building for national or global markets. With patient support from the state, a clear understanding of underserved users, and a willingness to take on problems few others are tackling, startups from smaller cities can design solutions that travel well beyond where they began.

If you or someone you know needs support, call Tele MANAS, the government’s free 24-hour mental health helpline, at 14416.

item.title: From selling drones to intelligence: Where will the next wave of value come from?
item.description: As the drone industry evolves, the focus is shifting from aircraft specifications to the value delivered to customers. The next phase of growth will be shaped by AI, software, integrated technologies and service-led business models.
item.content:encoded:
When we look at the value of a drone, it is easy to focus on the aircraft itself. How long can it fly? How much weight can it carry? How far can it travel? These are important questions, and they will continue to matter. But there is another question that deserves equal attention: what does the customer actually get from that flight?

A drone may spend several hours monitoring an area and return with a large volume of footage. Yet, if the operator has to spend several more hours reviewing that footage to identify something important, much of the benefit is lost. The real value lies not simply in collecting information, but in making sense of it and using it at the right time.

I believe this is where the next phase of the drone industry will take shape.

The value does not end when the drone lands

As drones become more widely used across defence, infrastructure, mapping, and homeland security, customer expectations are changing. Buying a drone is increasingly becoming the beginning of a larger operational requirement.

Consider a team monitoring a long stretch of border or inspecting a large infrastructure project. The drone can capture images, video and location data, but the customer needs more than these individual inputs. They need to know what has changed, whether something requires attention and what action should follow.

This is where software and artificial intelligence (AI) have a pivotal role to play. Automated video summaries, event detection, and searchable annotations can make it easier to find relevant information without having to watch hours of recordings. The idea is not to remove people from the decision-making process but to help them focus on what matters and make better-informed decisions.

Experience is difficult to replicate

There is something about technology that becomes clear only when it is used regularly in the field. A drone may perform well during testing, but actual operating conditions can be very different. Terrain, weather, temperature and connectivity can all affect how a system performs.

This is why the experience gained from real deployments matters. Across the industry, drone manufacturers are learning that building a reliable product is not just about getting the engineering right. It is also about understanding how customers use the technology, what difficulties they encounter and where improvements are needed.

The scale of deployments is important in this regard. Every mission provides an opportunity to understand how the aircraft, payload, software and communication systems perform in real conditions. Repeated operations can also reveal patterns that may not emerge during controlled testing.

Over time, this learning becomes an advantage. Companies that stay closely connected to actual operating conditions are better placed to develop technology that works outside controlled testing environments. It also helps them understand what customers need, rather than relying only on what they initially ask for.

Technology must work together

Intelligence is not limited to what happens to the data after a flight. It also depends on whether the drone can complete its mission reliably in the first place.

For instance, a drone operating in a challenging environment needs dependable communication and navigation. In defence applications, electronic interference, jamming and spoofing can create additional complications. Similarly, operations in remote locations may have limited network connectivity, making it important to process certain information closer to where it is collected.

This is why the industry needs to look at the entire technology stack rather than treating the aircraft, software, payload and communication systems as separate elements. Secure command-and-control systems, resilient navigation, edge computing and specialised payloads all contribute to the final outcome.

This shift is also reflected in India's evolving defence procurement priorities. The Defence Acquisition Council's recent approval of capital acquisition proposals worth approximately Rs 2.12 lakh crore includes requirements for Long Range UAS, Surveillance UAV, Integrated Surveillance and Strike Systems, and Long Range Kamikaze Drone Systems. With approximately 82% of the proposed procurements earmarked for the Indian industry, the direction is significant. It signals an opportunity for domestic manufacturers to move beyond building individual platforms towards developing integrated, mission-ready capabilities that address increasingly complex operational requirements.

This also helps reduce dependence on external technologies in areas where control, security and reliability are particularly important.

The business model will evolve with the technology

This shift also has implications for how drone companies build sustainable businesses. Hardware sales will remain an important part of the industry. However, the opportunity extends well beyond the initial sale of an aircraft. A drone has an operating lifecycle that involves software, analytics, maintenance, upgrades, training and support. Each of these can contribute to the value delivered to a customer over time.

Models such as Drone-as-a-Service, software subscriptions and analytics-led solutions can allow customers to access drone capabilities without having to manage every aspect of ownership and operations themselves. For providers, these models can create opportunities for longer-term customer relationships and a more diversified revenue mix.

From a business perspective, this also creates opportunities for repeat engagements and more predictable customer relationships. But these models will succeed only when they offer a clear economic or operational benefit. A customer will continue paying for a service if it helps reduce manual effort, improve efficiency or deliver information that was previously difficult to access.

The objective should not simply be to introduce more software or services. It should be to make the overall solution more useful to the customer.

The next opportunity is in delivering outcomes

The drone industry is still evolving, and there are challenges to address, particularly around data security, system integration, reliability and the economics of scaling these solutions. Not every application will require the same level of automation or intelligence. What matters is understanding the customer's actual requirement and developing technology accordingly.

As the market matures, I expect customers to place greater emphasis on the outcome rather than the specifications of the aircraft alone. They will want to know whether a drone can help them monitor an area more effectively, complete an inspection faster or respond to an incident with better information.

The aircraft will remain at the centre of this ecosystem, but it will be one part of a much larger solution. The companies that understand this shift early and invest in the right capabilities will be better positioned for the industry's next phase of growth.

Ultimately, the future of drones will not be determined only by how far they can fly or how long they can stay in the air but it will depend on how effectively every flight can be translated into intelligence, action and measurable value for the customer.

(Vipul Joshi is the CFO at ideaForge, an Indian aerospace and defense company)

item.title: NITES seeks policy framework to ringfence IT workers from AI job displacement
item.description: The Nascent Information Technology Employees Senate (NITES) is for technology moving forward the industry but not with leaving workforce behind
item.content:encoded:
The IT-union body NITES has called for a comprehensive policy framework to safeguard tech sector employees from job displacement arising from the uptake of Artificial Intelligence (AI), automation and other emerging technologies.

The Nascent Information Technology Employees Senate (NITES) has urged the government to initiate consultations with industry stakeholders and employee representatives to formulate such a forward-looking policy on responsible AI adoption and workforce protection, as it advocated that "technology should move the industry forward without leaving its workforce behind".

NITES acknowledged that technological advancement is important to the industry's growth, but added, in the same breath, that adoption of AI and automation must not leave employees without adequate notice, financial security or opportunities to move on to alternative employment.

It said that tech companies must be transparent when undertaking workforce reductions, particularly where such decisions are attributed to AI or automation.

Employees and government authorities must know how many people are affected, the reason behind their positions being eliminated and just how many jobs are directly being replaced by technology, it said in a release.

NITES has, in the past, raised its voice against mass layoffs, forced resignations and unfair employment practices in the IT sector.

While those earlier representations were not specifically focused on AI-related job losses, NITES believes the changing employment landscape now requires a dedicated policy framework to address this emerging challenge.

It has, accordingly, pitched for mandatory safeguards for affected employees.

"Employees should not be left to bear the entire burden of technological change. Companies adopting AI and automation should be required to provide reasonable advance notice, fair severance compensation and payment of all outstanding statutory and contractual dues," NITES said.

Further, employers should make all-out efforts to re-skill and redeploy existing employees within their organisations before eliminating their positions on account of technological advancements.

While existing labour laws provide certain retrenchment protection to eligible workers, NITES is of the view that stronger and more specific safeguards are necessary to address the challenges arising from AI-driven job displacement.

"Re-skilling must be meaningful and outcome-oriented. Merely providing access to online courses or training material cannot be considered adequate support," it said, exhorting employers to make genuine efforts to equip affected employees for alternative roles and future employment opportunities.

"The increasing impact of AI on employment now requires a dedicated policy-level discussion involving the government, Nasscom, IT companies and employee representatives," it said.

item.title: Zoho–LinkedIn report: AI is helping Indian SMBs grow, but skills lag behind
item.description: Zoho–LinkedIn report: Indian SMBs with AI talent grow teams 5.2 points faster, while only 6% have everyday AI skills across staff.
item.content:encoded:
Picture a typical Indian small-business founder. They run sales, approve leave requests and chase late payments. Their contacts are the company's biggest asset, and their WhatsApp is where most deals get done.

That model builds plenty of businesses, but it also caps how big they can get. The New Rules of Growth: How India's SMBs Are Building to Scale, a new joint report from Zoho and LinkedIn, looks at what happens when that cap arrives. Its answer: growing SMBs are moving work out of the founder's head and into systems, skills and teams.

The study covers July 2024 to June 2026. It combines LinkedIn network data from more than 1.4 billion members, including over 193 million in India, with usage data from more than 78,000 organisations on Zoho Workplace, Zoho People and Bigin by Zoho CRM. It defines an SMB as an India-headquartered business with 11 to 200 employees. The stakes are high: according to the Economic Survey 2025-26, SMBs contribute about 31% of India's GDP and nearly 49% of its exports.

The AI dividend is real

Rather than shrinking their workforce, SMBs that invest in AI talent are hiring faster. In the first half of 2026, Indian SMBs with in-house AI talent grew headcount 5.2 percentage points faster than other SMBs. That is more than double the 2.1-point gap among SMBs globally.

The lift isn't limited to software. Technology leads at 8.9 points, but construction (7.7), wholesale (7.3) and financial services (6.9) are close behind. The link is also strongest in smaller firms: among mid-market companies, the gap shrinks to 0.9 points.

"Those investing in AI talent are showing that AI and jobs can grow together," said Kumaresh Pattabiraman, India Country Manager at LinkedIn. The report adds a caveat: the data shows associations, not cause and effect.

The skills gap

The headline number has a weak spot. SMBs are better at building AI than at using it. LinkedIn data shows 16.3% have AI engineering skills in-house, but only 6.1% have everyday AI literacy across their workforce. Among large enterprises, the figures are more than 34% and 18%.

For most small businesses, everyday literacy matters more. A retailer or manufacturer doesn't need to build AI, but its people need to know how to use it. Pattabiraman's next step: make AI "a skill for every employee, not a specialist skill for a few."

Cautious by design

Part of the reason for the slow rollout is caution. AI-assisted search on Zoho Workplace has roughly doubled, and early adopters are using Bring-Your-Own-Key (BYOK) setups. These connect an AI model of the firm's choice using its own access key, so AI use stays within the contracts and data policies it already manages.

SMBs want the productivity of generative AI, but they are wary of sending sensitive data to outside providers. Use of password management tools has also risen about 35%.

Size matters too. Only 8.6% of micro-firms on Zoho People use AI in their HR tools, compared with 29.6% of larger SMBs. "Despite all the attention on AI, adoption still follows operational maturity," said Praval Singh, VP of Marketing and CX at Zoho.

When the founder is the sales team

More than 80,000 India-headquartered SMB founders on LinkedIn average over 1,300 connections each. Yet only about one in three SMBs has a formal sales leader at Director, VP or CXO level. In most firms, the founder is both head of sales and the face of the brand.

AI is helping lean teams go further. In the 12 months to June 2026, SMB sellers who used AI did roughly 40% more sales activity than those who didn't, and reached nearly twice as many decision-makers. They also grew their networks faster: in the year after adopting AI, their monthly new connections rose 40%, against 31% for similar sellers who didn't.

Meanwhile, routine sales work is moving into software, from the first chat to the final payment. Bigin by Zoho CRM data shows:

  • Workflow automation rose about 42%, routing new leads and flagging stalled deals automatically.
  • Payment link usage grew about 56%, helping customers pay as soon as a deal is agreed.
  • WhatsApp messages sent through the CRM rose almost sixfold, as deals move to mobile and to the channels buyers already use.

Earning trust in public

Buyers now size up a business long before they talk to it, and more SMBs are making sure they can be found.

Monthly active SMB advertisers on LinkedIn grew about 13% year on year, and click-through rates rose roughly 81%. The most engaging 10% of advertisers keep campaigns running 26% longer and use 83% more ad creatives than the bottom 10%. About one in six SMB advertisers now mention AI in their ads, mostly as "AI-powered" or "AI-driven" rather than "AI-native."

The 50-employee wall

In HR, the tipping point comes at about 50 employees. Below it, attendance lives on a spreadsheet and leave is approved in a WhatsApp group. Beyond it, informal processes start to fail. Among Zoho People customers, 68% of larger SMBs use several advanced HR features, against just 9% of micro-firms. About 16% of SMBs on the platform use its AI assistant to handle routine HR queries.

Founders want tools that fit how they already work. Custom workflows (about 35%) and custom modules (27%) are the most used advanced features, well ahead of ready-made ones such as performance management (14%).

Hiring wider, and further away

Skills-based hiring widens the search. Employers in India that hire for skills rather than job titles or degrees can reach 11 times more candidates, and 22 times more for AI roles.

SMBs are also hiring across borders. Their share of hires made outside India rose from about 22% to nearly 27% between 2025 and 2026, led by the US, UAE, UK and Nigeria.

What it adds up to

The report doesn't describe a sweeping transformation. It describes steady, practical progress. Indian SMBs are adopting technology one function at a time and building systems around the people who already make the business work. For founders, the lessons are clear:

  • Start with one workflow, such as sales follow-ups or routine HR questions.
  • Put guardrails in place first, within your existing permissions and data policies.
  • Build systems before you reach 50 employees, not after things start to break.
  • Teach AI to everyone, not just a few specialists.

As Singh put it, the priority is "building the skills to use it well, so they can scale without losing agility." The founder's network still opens the first doors. What this report shows is what it takes to keep growing after that.

item.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 26, 2026)
item.description: YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Thursday, November 26, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Uber India gets a new head as investors continue to invest in Indian startups, YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors.

Featured stories

Uber appoints former Zomato CEO Rakesh Ranjan as President for India, South Asia

Uber has appointed former Zomato food delivery CEO Rakesh Ranjan as President for India and South Asia, effective January 4, 2027.

Ranjan joined Zomato in 2017 and spent eight years at the company. During his tenure, he led its food ordering and delivery business as CEO, having previously held leadership roles across Zomato Gold and sales.

Read more

HC to hear on Friday Tata Trusts’ pleas against Chandrasekaran’s reappointment

The Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and the R.D. Tata Trust (RDTT) on Thursday filed suits in the Bombay High Court against Tata Sons and six of its directors, challenging the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as executive chairman for a third five-year term. The court will hear the matter on Friday. The SDTT has sought Rs 50 crore, while the RDTT has sought Rs 15 crore in damages, with 18 per cent annual interest.

Read more

Funding news

Finnable raises Rs 405 Cr in Series C to expand multi-product lending

Fintech company Finnable has raised Rs 405 crore in a Series C round from Bharat Value Fund, part of the Pantomath Group, Pratithi Investments and NKSquared. Existing backers Z47, TVS Capital and Claypond Capital continue in the company.

Read more

Green Aero raises $14M as India pushes for indigenous jet propulsion

Green Aero, an aerospace and defence startup has raised $14 million in a Series A round led by Crane Ventures. The other participants were 3one4 Capital, Antler Elevate, and pi Ventures.

Read more

Other news

CredAble acquires 70% stake in AI regulatory intelligence platform Reql

CredAble, a working capital and banking technology platform, has acquired a 70% stake in Reql, an AI-native regulatory intelligence platform, expanding its presence in the regulatory technology (RegTech) segment. Reql helps banks, financial institutions and corporates automate regulatory research, policy gap analysis and compliance management. Its platform monitors official regulatory sources in real time and captures new circulars, enabling organisations to assess their impact and track compliance actions.

The company aims to reduce the time required to close compliance actions from as much as 60 days to less than four hours. CredAble plans to leverage its network of over 100 banking partners and 175 corporate clients to expand Reql's adoption. It expects the platform to contribute 25% of consolidated revenue over the next 24 to 36 months.

Panasonic, IvyCap launch IGNITION Challenge 2.0 for Indian startups

Panasonic Life Solutions India has launched the second edition of its IGNITION Challenge in partnership with IvyCap Ventures to accelerate the adoption of hyperspectral camera technology in India. The initiative will connect Panasonic's advanced imaging technology with Indian startups and innovators to develop applications across healthcare, agriculture, industrial quality, energy and food manufacturing. The programme will combine hyperspectral imaging, artificial intelligence and domain-specific expertise to address industry challenges.

IvyCap Ventures will lead startup sourcing and ecosystem engagement, while Panasonic's India Innovation Centre will oversee programme design and evaluation. The initiative aims to shortlist six to eight startups for technical evaluation. It will culminate in a Demo Day in March 2027, with three to four potential co-development partners expected to be selected.

Biz2X partners with SIDBI to strengthen digital lending operations

Biz2X, a digital lending platform and subsidiary of Biz2Credit, has partnered with the Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) to streamline lending operations and improve credit delivery to MSMEs. Under the partnership, Biz2X will provide its lending customer relationship management platform to consolidate leads generated through multiple channels, including WhatsApp, direct selling agents, OEM partners and marketing campaigns.

The platform offers AI-powered BizBot for pipeline insights, management dashboards to monitor conversions and productivity, and mobile applications to support field teams. The initiative comes amid growing demand for formal MSME credit. According to the July 2026 MSME Pulse report, outstanding commercial credit balances reached ₹65.8 lakh crore in March 2026, registering 14% annual growth. However, only 41% of registered MSMEs have accessed formal credit.

Australian retailer Officeworks opens GCC in Bengaluru

Australian omnichannel retailer Officeworks has inaugurated its Global Capability Centre (GCC) at Manyata Tech Park in Bengaluru as part of its multi-year business transformation strategy. The centre, operating as Officeworks Bengaluru, will work alongside the company's Melbourne support office to strengthen capabilities in data, digital technology, artificial intelligence and retail operations.

The Bengaluru team will support functions including merchandising, customer operations, finance, analytics, AI, digital engineering and core retail platforms such as SAP and Salesforce. It will also contribute to developing omnichannel customer experiences and improving operational efficiency.

94% of Indian brands fail basic AI website readiness test: Publive-IAMAI study

A study by AI visibility infrastructure company Publive and the Internet and Mobile Association of India (IAMAI) has found that 94% of India's leading brands fail the basic test of website readability by artificial intelligence systems. The study, titled Can AI Read India Inc.?, examined 951 mid-market and enterprise brands across sectors including automotive, financial services, consumer durables, hotels and B2B SaaS. Only one brand achieved strong AI readiness.

The findings show that AI bots receive 84% code and just 16% actual content from the median brand website. Additionally, 48 brands provide no readable content to AI crawlers. The study highlights the need for businesses to improve website structures and introduce structured data so AI platforms can accurately understand and represent their brands.

Dhan launches free AI-powered charting platform TradingCharts

Raise Financial Services, the parent company of stockbroking platform Dhan, has launched TradingCharts, an AI-powered charting platform designed for Indian traders and investors. Developed entirely in-house, the platform offers more than 20 chart types, 200 indicators, eight chart layouts and multiple timeframes. It also includes advanced tools such as Order Flow, Volume Profile, Depth of Market and Bar Replay. TradingCharts provides real-time market data across enabled NSE, BSE and MCX segments when connected to a brokerage platform. Dhan’s Fuzz AI assistant allows users to create indicators and trading strategies through natural-language prompts. The platform also features an Indicator Marketplace where creators can monetise their tools.

Chariot launches indigenous AI foundation models under IndiaAI Mission

Chariot Artificial Intelligence has launched its Chariot-1 foundation models under the IndiaAI Mission, marking a development in India's efforts to build indigenous AI capabilities. The models include an 11-billion-parameter large language model and a text-to-speech system supporting English and 10 Indian languages. Both were pretrained from scratch in India. The company has introduced three research innovations: IndicShift, which improves processing across Indian scripts; Nested Training, which enables multiple model sizes to be trained simultaneously; and Mixture of Vocabularies, which improves training efficiency.

Chariot-1 is available in three model sizes to support deployment across data centres, laptops, smartphones and edge devices. Its speech model has recorded over 97% verbalisation accuracy in the reported benchmark tests. The launch was inaugurated by MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan.

Wadhwani Foundation invites applications for employment and livelihood grants

Wadhwani Foundation has invited Expressions of Interest from organisations across India for grants aimed at expanding job creation, employment and livelihood opportunities. Through Wadhwani Grants, the foundation plans to provide multi-year funding over three to five years, with support linked to independently verified outcomes such as job placements, jobs created and improvements in household incomes.

The initiative targets organisations working in three areas: job fulfilment through skilling and placement, job creation through entrepreneurship and MSME growth, and livelihood upliftment for self-employed individuals and households. The grants will complement existing funding without equity dilution or repayment obligations. Selected organisations will also receive free access to the foundation's AI-powered GenieAI platform and its wider technology ecosystem. The foundation aims to help proven organisations multiply their impact by two to three times.

ACKO brings insurance innovations to life through entertainment-led Purple Carpet

Digital insurance company ACKO has hosted The Purple Carpet, an entertainment-led brand experience to showcase its latest innovations across motor, health and travel insurance. Designed around a film-premiere format rather than a conventional product launch, the event brought together MS Dhoni, Javed Akhtar, Farah Khan and more than 60 creators and comedians.

One of the key attractions was 'Where's the Saboot?', a courtroom-style game show featuring ACKO Drivecam footage and performances by comedians and creators. The event also included stand-up comedy sets highlighting ACKO Drivecam-linked car insurance, ACKO Air Pass and ACKO Clinic. A conversation between Dhoni and Javed Akhtar explored clarity of purpose and intention in the context of insurance. ACKO said the initiative reflects its strategy of using entertainment and storytelling to make insurance more relevant to consumers.

Axis Communications expands BIS-certified camera portfolio in India

Axis Communications has expanded its portfolio of BIS-ER-01 certified network cameras in India, securing certification for nine additional models. This takes its total certified portfolio in the country to 20 models. The latest certifications cover multiple product families as the company strengthens its compliance with India's regulatory and cybersecurity requirements. Its M-Series camera model AXIS M4216-LV is already available in India, while additional models across the P14 and P32 series are progressing through the certification process.

SpotDraft appoints Sajana Shankaran as VP of Human Resources

AI-native contract lifecycle management platform SpotDraft has appointed Sajana Shankaran as Vice President of Human Resources as it prepares for its next phase of global expansion. Shankaran will lead the company's people strategy across the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and India, focusing on organisational development, talent capabilities and building scalable structures. She brings more than 20 years of experience in strategic HR leadership and joins SpotDraft from Branch, where she served as Director, HR Business Partner and Head of People Partner for APAC.

Atovio launches wearable air purifier for children

Indian wearable technology startup Atovio has launched Atovio Nino, a wearable air purifier designed for children aged four and above. Priced at Rs 3,499, Nino uses ion technology without a filter or fan to address airborne particles, including PM2.5 and PM10. It offers three operating modes and provides up to 72 hours of battery life on a full charge. The company said laboratory tests at IIT Kanpur recorded a 90% reduction in airborne particle concentration within 25 minutes in a sealed chamber.

item.title: XEBO.ai bags $10.5M funding from Emirates Growth Fund
item.description: The capital injection will primarily enhance XEBO voice-of-customer portfolio, expanding capability into call analytics and digital experience monitoring. A key portion of the funding will advance agentic AI.
item.content:encoded:
Dubai-headquartered technology firm XEBO.ai has raised $10.5 million in Series A funding from the Emirates Growth Fund, marking the sovereign investor as its first institutional partner.

Founded in 2017 by Yash Sultania and Anand Nigam, XEBO is an AI-native experience management platform that converts customer and employee feedback into decision-ready insights. Experience management platforms help organisations capture feedback across surveys, social listening and customer journey mapping to guide strategic operational decisions.

The capital injection will primarily enhance XEBO voice-of-customer portfolio, expanding capability into call analytics and digital experience monitoring. A key portion of the funding will advance agentic AI.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Yash Sultania explained that the investment enables the team to “deepen our VoC portfolio, with agentic AI at its core, and take it to customers around the world faster”.

Beyond software development, the firm plans to expand its commercial operations across the Gulf Cooperation Council region, establish a presence in the United States, and recruit senior operational leaders.

The company also intends to leverage technology integrations with partner channels such as Microsoft to widen enterprise reach. Co-founder Anand Nigam noted that the backing allows the firm to “drive technology innovation, strengthen our presence in existing markets and expand into new geographies as we scale globally”.

The experience management sector has historically been dominated by legacy global platforms, but XEBO has built traction with over 350 enterprise clients across banking, aviation, telecommunications and healthcare. Operating from offices in the United States, the UAE, India and Saudi Arabia, the company has received industry recognition from analyst firms Gartner, IDC and Forrester.

Anshul Garg, Investment Director at Emirates Growth Fund, highlighted that XEBO managed to “build an innovative product that addresses a real market need” while demonstrating relevance alongside established global players.

The Emirates Growth Fund represents the flagship growth equity investor of the United Arab Emirates. Launched by Dr Sultan Al Jaber at Make it in the Emirates 2025 and backed by Emirates Development Bank, it stands as the only UAE sovereign fund focused exclusively on growth-stage enterprises through strategic minority equity investments.

Matthew Singh, Chief Investment Officer at Emirates Growth Fund, noted that the firm “has proven itself with leading enterprises in demanding markets” and remains “well placed to scale internationally”.

item.title: Dough, design, drool: food entrepreneurship insights from Bakery Business 2026
item.description: In this photo essay from Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai, we showcase food industry highlights from the exhibition halls along with insights for innovators.
item.content:encoded:
Launched in 2014, PhotoSparks is a weekly feature from YourStory, with photographs that celebrate the spirit of creativity and innovation. In the earlier 1,040 posts, we featured an art festival, cartoon gallery. world music festival, telecom expo, millets fair, climate change expo, wildlife conference, startup festival, Diwali rangoli, and jazz festival.

Looking to begin your entrepreneurial journey in the food space? A good event for product insights, industry trends, and professional networking would be the 19th annual edition of the Bakery Business trade show, being held this week at the Jio World Convention Centre, BKC, Mumbai.

Organised by Hospitality First, it is held alongside the 14th annual HoReCa Business exhibition for the hospitality, restaurants and catering industry. With around 200 exhibitors, it reportedly attracted 15,000 business visitors.

As seen in this photo essay, it features not just cutting-edge technology and ingredients, but also demonstrations and competitions. For example, The India Pizza Championship brought together talented pizzaiolos (artisan pizza chefs) from across the country to showcase their skills on a national platform.

Such events point to a number of trends in this space for food entrepreneurs: the rise of cloud kitchens, the combination of bakeries with indulgent dining experiences, the growth of institutional investment, and the proliferation of bakery and restaurant chains that involve central kitchens and heavy automation.

In this photo essay, we showcase some of the exhibitors at Bakery Business 2026, such as Mahe to the World, Tandoor King, Mavee's, Mala's, Stagioni, Celebre, Ecolane, Morde, Pro Dough, Bakersville, and others.

Also Read
2026 Outlook: AI, robotics, biotech, unicorns and the road ahead

Tandoor King International is a Mumbai-based manufacturer and supplier of commercial tandoors and baking equipment. Its product range includes stainless-steel tandoors, mild-steel tandoors, clay tandoors, gas-operated tandoors, and charcoal tandoors.

Mahe is a new premium bakery brand launched by Bikaji Foods International in partnership with master baker TK Khaleel. It aims to bring European baking traditions and artisanal craftsmanship to the Indian market, via offerings such as semi-finished bakery bases that foodservice operators can customise.

Morde Foods is a leading manufacturer of chocolate and cocoa-based products, with a strong presence in the B2B segment. It supplies compound chocolates, chocolate fillings, spreads, toppings, decorations, and inclusions to chocolatiers and restaurants.

Bakersville India is a prominent supplier and manufacturer of bakery ingredients, food decoration products, baking tools, and food packaging solutions. It has developed a substantial distribution network across India, and operates retail outlets under the Food Décor Shop name.

Mala’s, based in Panchgani near Mahabaleshwar, is famous for its strawberry and fruit jams, crushes, syrups, sauces, and fresh fruit treats. It is a major fruit-product manufacturer with pan-India distribution and exports to over 20 countries.

Meeting such exhibitors and large players helps aspiring food entrepreneurs explore opportunities to launch new offerings, improve product quality, and differentiate their menu. They can evaluate how technology can improve consistency, reduce wastage, save labour, and increase production capacity.

Also Read
How IIT Madras Incubation Cell is powering India’s next-gen deeptech startups

Such technologies include commercial ovens, mixers, processing machinery, refrigeration, and automation solutions. They can help improve operating economics for standalone and chain systems.

The food ecosystem is enriched by a wide range of business models. Entrepreneurs can explore opportunities via bakery cafés, central kitchens, QSRs, and cloud kitchens. Such models help understand how new businesses can diversify beyond traditional retail sales.

Meeting ingredient manufacturers, equipment suppliers, distributors, and fellow entrepreneurs helps forge new relationships. Live demonstrations, professional competitions and knowledge activities can spur innovation in product categories.

In sum, such industry exhibitions help entrepreneurs benchmark prices, calculate the unit economics, discover new products, and explore the use of automation. They enable identification of growth opportunities and ideas for product lines.

The overall opportunity at such a trade show is not simply to buy better equipment or ingredients. It is to rethink how to launch, improve and scale a food business in a fast-changing world with ever-increasing customer expectations.

Now what have you done today to pause in your busy schedule and harness your creative side for a better world?

(All photographs taken by Madanmohan Rao on location at Bakery Business 2026.)

item.title: GIVA raises Rs 90 Cr from alternative credit platform BlackSoil
item.description: GIVA said it will use the capital to fund store expansion and working capital requirements as it strengthens its omnichannel presence across India.
item.content:encoded:
Jewellery brand GIVA has raised Rs 90 crore from alternative credit platform BlackSoil. This comes less than a month after the company announced a funding round of over $100 million led by Multiples Alternate Asset Management, alongside existing investors Epiq Capital and Edelweiss Discovery Fund.

The capital will support GIVA's store-related capital expenditure and working capital requirements as the company expands its retail network and strengthens its omnichannel presence, it said in a statement.

Founded in 2019 and headquartered in Bengaluru, GIVA focuses on everyday jewellery, catering primarily to Indian consumers. The brand is backed by several prominent celebrities, including Kriti Sanon and Anushka Sharma. Its portfolio spans 92.5 silver, gold, gold-plated, rose gold-plated, and lab-grown diamond jewellery.

GIVA follows an omnichannel distribution model through its own retail stores, D2C website and third-party ecommerce and quick-commerce marketplaces. The company has also been expanding its manufacturing capabilities and offline presence.

“As we continue to grow GIVA's retail presence, building the right financial and operational capabilities is important to supporting our expansion. Our partnership with BlackSoil will support our store expansion plans and working capital requirements as we scale our omnichannel business. We continue to focus on making design-led jewellery more accessible to consumers while building a wider and stronger retail network across India,” said Ishendra Agarwal, Founder & CEO, GIVA.

"GIVA has established a strong brand presence in India's D2C jewellery space, supported by its product range, growth and omnichannel presence. Its strong brand recognition, performance as well as association with reputed investors made it a compelling prospect to support. The funding from us will enable GIVA to meet its expansion and working capital requirements," said Ankur Bansal, Managing Director, BlackSoil.

The company currently retails through more than 400 stores across India and Sri Lanka.

item.title: HC to hear on Friday Tata Trusts’ pleas against Chandrasekaran’s reappointment
item.description: The lawsuit by the Tata Trusts says the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as Tata Sons Chairman was invalid as it did not receive the affirmative vote required.
item.content:encoded:
The Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and the R.D. Tata Trust (RDTT) on Thursday filed suits in the Bombay High Court against Tata Sons and six of its directors, challenging the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as executive chairman for a third five-year term.

The court will hear the matter on Friday.

The SDTT has sought Rs 50 crore, while the RDTT has sought Rs 15 crore in damages, with 18 per cent annual interest.

As per the suits, the September 17 Tata Sons board resolution to reappoint Chandrasekaran was invalid because it did not receive the affirmative vote required under Article 121 of the company’s Articles of Association (AoA).

Senior counsel Janak Dwarkadas, appearing for the two trusts, mentioned the suits on Thursday before a single bench of Justice Arif Doctor, seeking an urgent hearing.

Justice Doctor, however, recused himself without assigning any reasons, following which the suits were mentioned before Justice Abhay Ahuja, who was sitting on the alternate bench.

Dwarkadas told the court that a hearing was required before the November 30 board meeting of Tata Sons.

Justice Ahuja then said the pleas shall be heard on Friday.

The immediate relief sought is to prevent the chairman of Tata Sons from exercising his casting vote during the November 30 board meeting in the event of a split in opinion among nominee directors.

In the suits, the trusts have not sought a stay on the board meeting but a direction that Chandrasekaran does not cast his vote.

The suits said Article 121 of Tata Sons’ AoA does not permit the chairman of a board meeting to exercise a casting vote in cases where the articles require the affirmative vote of a majority of the trustees.

The dispute follows N Chandrasekaran’s reappointment as Tata Sons executive chairman for five more years at the September 17 board meeting.

The suits have said the decision was “ultra vires the Articles of Association and is invalid, illegal, null and void”.

The two trusts voted on Wednesday night to pass the resolutions to move HC as there was a lack of any satisfactory replies to the communications sent by them since September 17.

Tata Trusts, chaired by Noel Tata, holds around 66 per cent of Tata Sons and has sought a permanent order and injunction restraining Tata Sons, its directors, officers and other agents from acting upon in any manner or giving effect to the September 17 resolution reappointing Chandrasekaran.

In a statement on September 20, the Trusts had said the resolution was not validly passed and had no legal effect.

At the centre of the dispute are Tata Sons’ AoA and special rights given to Trusts-nominated directors. It has two nominee directors on its board -- Noel Tata and Venu Srinivasan. On September 17, Noel Tata had voted against Chandrasekaran’s reappointment, while Venu Srinivasan supported it.

item.title: Uber appoints former Zomato CEO Rakesh Ranjan as President for India, South Asia
item.description: Ranjan, who spent eight years at Zomato, will take charge of Uber’s India and South Asia operations from January 4, 2027.
item.content:encoded:
Uber has appointed former Zomato food delivery CEO Rakesh Ranjan as President for India and South Asia, effective January 4, 2027, as the mobility platform looks to strengthen its presence in one of its largest global markets.

Ranjan will report to Dom Taylor, Uber’s Regional General Manager for Asia Pacific. He joins Uber from Allen Online, where he currently serves as CEO.

Ranjan joined Zomato in 2017 and spent eight years at the company. During his tenure, he led its food ordering and delivery business as CEO, having previously held leadership roles across Zomato Gold and sales.

“Uber has built a business that matters to how people move and earn across India and South Asia. The opportunity ahead is significant, and it starts with the everyday experience: dependable rides, value across different journeys and better earning opportunities for drivers. I’m excited to join the talented team and build on a great foundation,” said Ranjan in a statement.

Announcing the appointment, Taylor said: “After a search spanning more than three months, we’re delighted to welcome Rakesh to Uber. We set a high bar for this role, and his experience running large consumer businesses in India, combined with his ambition for what comes next, stood out."

"India and South Asia matter enormously to Uber’s future. Rakesh joins a business with real scale and enduring strength and he brings valuable experience to lead the next chapter of growth and innovation for our business in the region,” Taylor added.

India is Uber’s third-largest market globally by trips, after the US and Brazil, and its second-largest by the number of earners. The company operates in more than 225 cities across the country, offering multiple mobility options, including bikes, autos, cars and metro services. More than two million monthly active drivers earn through its platform.

India is also home to Uber’s largest technology centres outside the US, located in Bengaluru and Hyderabad. The company entered the Indian market in 2013 and has since expanded its presence across mobility categories.

item.title: Vardhaman Jain: Who is the industrialist behind Tirumala’s gold donation?
item.description: Vardhaman Jain, a Chennai-based entrepreneur linked to Access Healthcare and Asia Engineering, has donated 121 kg of gold ornaments worth Rs 206 crore to Tirumala.
item.content:encoded:
A donation of 121 kg of gold is difficult to overlook. But behind the Rs 206 crore offering made to Venkateswara at Tirumala is a businessman whose career has largely unfolded in healthcare services and Asia engineering and technology.

Chennai-based industrialist and philanthropist Vardhaman Jain, along with his wife Radhika Jain, made the offering on Thursday, November 26, 2026. The donation comprises 46 gold ornaments and is among the largest contributions received by Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD).

The ornaments were presented in the presence of Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu and senior TTD officials. They were first displayed at Ranganayakula Mandapam before being ceremonially taken to the sanctum sanctorum.

From building healthcare services businesses to taking up leadership roles in large technology companies, Vardhaman Jain's professional journey has covered several areas. Here's a look at the entrepreneur behind the offering.

From Vision HealthSource to Access Healthcare

Before Access Healthcare became a part of his business journey, Vardhaman had already worked in the healthcare services industry. He co-founded Vision HealthSource, a healthcare services company that was acquired by Perot Systems in 2003.

Following the acquisition, he held senior positions at Perot Systems and Dell Services. His responsibilities included managing director of Dell Services' BPO operations, giving him experience in managing large-scale business process services.

In 2011, he went on to establish Access Healthcare with Shaji Ravi and others. The company provides technology-enabled revenue cycle management services to healthcare providers, primarily in the US. Its offerings cover medical billing, coding, accounts receivable management, analytics and automation-led services. The company has also had Anurag Jain as its chairman and CEO, while Shaji Ravi has served as founder, president and managing director.

Healthcare services are not the only area in which Vardhaman has worked. His professional interests also include business process automation and technology development. Public company profiles credit him with patents related to medical image processing and the use of data extracted from electronic images.

Vardhaman studied statistics at Loyola College in Chennai before pursuing computer science at the University of Texas at Austin.

A career that extends beyond business

Alongside his business interests, Vardhaman has been associated with initiatives in healthcare, education and skill development.

His philanthropic work includes the Shree Sarita Jain Foundation Trust and Aavishkaar, a skill-development initiative for underprivileged youth. He is also listed as the managing trustee of Kanchi Kamakoti CHILDS Trust Hospital.

His association with Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams is not limited to the latest offering. Earlier contributions include electric buses for pilgrim transport and financial support for the Sri Venkateswara Bhakti Channel, besides other temple-related initiatives.

What went into the 121-kg offering?

According to TTD, the couple's donation used 121 kg of 24-carat gold to prepare ornaments for two temples. Of this, 106 kg was used for jewellery intended for Venkateswara at Tirumala, while the remaining 15 kg will go towards a vastram for Sri Padmavathi Ammavari at the Tiruchanoor temple.

The collection includes a crown, necklaces, anklets, armlets, waist ornaments, hand ornaments and pada kavachams, along with covers for the conch and chakra. Diamonds, blue and yellow sapphires, rubies, emeralds and saligrama stones also feature in the ornaments.

The Rs 206 crore offering has brought Vardhaman's philanthropic contributions into the spotlight. Yet, his work across healthcare, technology, education and temple initiatives shows that his interests extend well beyond a single business or industry.

item.title: Agnikul’s rocket ambitions gather pace, but commercial revenue yet to take off
item.description: The spacetech company is investing heavily in its launch ambitions and attracting fresh funding, but, with no operating revenue yet, commercialisation remains its biggest test.
item.content:encoded:
Agnikul Cosmos is continuing to build the technology and infrastructure for a private launch business. But its FY26 audited accounts show that the financial returns from its efforts are yet to materialise.

The Chennai-based spactech company reported no revenue from operations for the fourth consecutive financial year, even as its spending and investment commitments increased.

For the year ended March 31, 2026, Agnikul reported a net loss of Rs 60.22 crore, against Rs 54.79 crore in FY25. Total income fell 22.5% to Rs 6.04 crore. Crucially, almost all of this came from interest on fixed deposits, which contributed Rs 5.83 crore.

Total expenses rose 25.2% to Rs 66.27 crore. Employee benefits accounted for Rs 29.37 crore, while other expenses came to Rs 29.15 crore. Cash used in operating activities increased to Rs 58.50 crore from Rs 36.73 crore. The figures show the cost of maintaining a technical workforce and developing a complex hardware business before commercial operations begin.

The balance sheet points to continued investment. Capital work-in-progress increased to Rs 82.63 crore from Rs 51.30 crore, while property, plant and equipment rose to Rs 34.29 crore from Rs 16.13 crore.

The group also disclosed Rs 121.84 crore of outstanding commitments for capital expenditure, against Rs 17.82 crore a year earlier. Cash and bank balances stood at Rs 105.22 crore, although only Rs 13.76 crore was classified as cash and cash equivalents.

Agnikul has, however, made progress on the technology front. Its Agnibaan SOrTeD mission, launched on May 30, 2024, was a sub-orbital technology demonstration that tested its indigenous systems, including a single-piece 3D-printed engine. The flight, from the company’s privately developed launchpad at Sriharikota, was an important milestone.

Also Read
The next frontier: Agnikul Cosmos bets on 3D-printed rocket engines for affordable space launches

There are also signs of a shift towards commercial applications. In February, Agnikul announced a multi-mission, multi-year agreement with Bengaluru-based NeevCloud to launch and host an orbital AI data-centre module using Agnibaan’s extendable upper stage.

Co-founder and CEO Srinath Ravichandran noted that the agreement would extend over three to four years. Its financial value was not disclosed. The initial plan was to prototype the concept in 2026, with deployment targeted for mid-2027.

Ravichandran has also outlined ambitions to achieve profitability within two years and scale up to 50 launches annually by 2030, subject to market demand and available capacity. The company is exploring a business model that combines launch fees with recurring income from hosting customer equipment on orbital platforms.

Agnikul’s next launch is expected in the first half of 2027, with the company indicating that it will demonstrate reusable launch-vehicle and upper-stage technologies.

Meanwhile, on September 25, 2026, the Technology Development Board, under the Department of Science and Technology, announced Rs 200 crore in financial support under the Research, Development and Innovation Fund for developing a fully reusable Agnibaan launch vehicle. The support, structured through optionally convertible debentures, aims to advance the technology from Technology Readiness Level 4 and above towards Level 8.

Agnikul has demonstrated that it can build and fly an indigenous rocket technology demonstrator, while beginning to establish commercial relationships. The challenge now is to turn these advances into repeatable missions, paying customers, and sustainable revenue.
